newsitem.title: USA: Scientists urge more safeguards for space station.
newsitem.headline: Scientists urge more safeguards for space station.

text.p: To avoid being battered by debris, the planned international space station will need effective shields and the ability to perform the space equivalent of fancy footwork, a report issued on Wednesday said.

The report by a National Research Council panel said some portions of the space station on which construction is to begin this year would be particularly vulnerable to damage from collisions with meteoroids and space debris.

The station will have shields to protect it and ground-based sensors will track large debris so the station can move out of the path of danger. But most debris is too small to be picked up by those sensors and more research is needed on the shields, particularly for the vulnerable portions of the station where the initial crew will live, the report said.
The United States, Russia, Canada, Japan and the European Space Agency will participate in building the space station.

"Overall efforts to protect the space station have been extensive and thorough," committee chairman George Gleghorn, a retired vice president of the TRW Space and Technology Group, said. "However, the space station will be particularly vulnerable to collisions because of its size and because it will be in orbit for at least 15 years."

In addition to improving safety features, the panel cited a need for more international cooperation to limit the amount of new debris, such as satellite fragments, left in space from other missions. It also said the crew's space suits must be re-assessed to make sure they are resistant to punctures.

It called for better emergency procedures to design early warning systems to protect crew members and to deal with potential problems from damage to solar energy cells, wiring, pipes or other essential systems.
